extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing MPEP §2106 guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether claim additional elements amount to 'significantly more' than a judicial exception under §101 (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B), including how to evaluate whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional, or otherwise meaningful limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a determination whether the additional elements in a claim amount to significantly more than a judicial exception, the examiner should evaluate whether the elements define only well-understood, routine, conventional activity; this consideration overlaps with improvement, mere instructions to apply an exception, and insignificant extra-solution activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess additional elements individually and in combination; use other Step 2B considerations (MPEP §2106.05(a), (f), (g)) to assist. If elements or functions are beyond those recognized in the art or courts as well-understood/routine/conventional, they will in most cases favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known-in-the-art elements can still be unconventional/non-routine
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination of additional elements) that is known in the art can nonetheless be unconventional or non-routine such that it amounts to significantly more than a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty/obviousness under §§102/103 is a separate inquiry; an improvement over conventional functionality can render a claim eligible even if not novel over the prior art (example: Enfish describing a self-referential database that provided technical improvements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual determination required to conclude an element is well-understood, routine, conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: A factual determination is required to support a conclusion that an additional element (or combination) is well-understood, routine, conventional activity; examiners should rely on what courts or those skilled in the art would recognize as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prior art search is not always necessary; the specification may indicate elements are conventional. The required factual determination must be expressly supported in writing. Appropriate support includes: (a) citation to specification or applicant statement; (b) citation to court decisions noting conventional nature; (c) citation to publications showing conventional nature; (d) an examiner's official notice. See MPEP §2106.07(a) for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of conventional additional elements may provide an inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if one or more additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional when considered individually, their combination may amount to an inventive concept (i.e., significantly more than the judicial exception).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a new combination produces a non-conventional/non-generic arrangement or technical improvement (examples: Diamond v. Diehr; Rapid Litigation Management v. CellzDirect; BASCOM). Examiners should only reject when, based on their expertise, they can conclude the additional elements do not amount to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection standard for Step 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if an examiner, relying on their expertise in the art, can conclude in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to significantly more (i.e., Step 2B: NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If elements/functions are beyond those recognized as well-understood/routine/conventional, they will typically amount to significantly more (Step 2B: YES). Document analysis on the record when concluding elements meaningfully limit the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized computer functions that can be well-understood/routine/conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts have recognized certain computer functions as well-understood, routine, and conventional when claimed in a generic manner or as insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., receiving/transmitting data over a network; performing repetitive calculations; electronic recordkeeping; storing and retrieving information in memory; scanning/extracting data; web browser navigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cited cases: Symantec; TLI Communications; OIP Techs.; buySAFE; DDR Holdings (distinguishing cases where specific manipulation yields a technical result). Listing is illustrative, not exhaustive — a generic recitation of these functions may weigh against eligibility, but specific non-generic implementations can be eligible (see DDR, BASCOM, Amdocs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-recognized life-science/laboratory techniques that can be well-understood/routine/conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: In the life sciences, courts have recognized laboratory techniques as conventional when claimed at a high level of generality (e.g., determining biomarker levels in blood; using PCR to amplify/detect DNA; detecting DNA/enzymes; immunizing a patient; analyzing DNA sequences; freezing and thawing cells; amplifying/sequencing nucleic acids; hybridizing gene probes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases include Mayo; Cleveland Clinic; Genetic Technologies; Ariosa/Sequenom; Rapid Litigation Management; Ambry Genetics. Generic recitation of such techniques may be insufficient to render claims eligible; specific unconventional applications may favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other activities courts have found well-understood/routine/conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found other high-level activities to be conventional when recited generically (examples: recording a customer's order; shuffling/dealing a standard deck of cards; restricting public access by requiring ad viewing; presenting offers and gathering statistics; determining estimated outcomes and prices; arranging/sorting information for pricing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples (from Apple v. Ameranth; In re Smith; Ultramercial; OIP Techs.; Versata) illustrate that routine business or clerical activities claimed at a high level typically do not add significantly more, absent specific technical integration or unconventional arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations — require limits beyond mere technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim should add meaningful limitations beyond generally linking the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment to transform the exception into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful limitations include considerations discussed in MPEP §2106.05(a)-(d) when they amount to significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application. Examples: Diehr (Arrhenius equation applied within an automated rubber-molding process) and Classen (analysis plus a concrete immunization step). Avoid claims that only implement the exception via generic computer components (Alice). Consider treatment/prophylaxis overlap with Step 2A Prong Two (MPEP §2106.04(d)(2)). Examiners should analyze elements both individually and in combination and explain on the record where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements that amount to nothing more than an instruction to 'apply' an abstract idea, law of nature, or other judicial exception (or equivalent) — e.g., 'apply it' on a computer — do not render the claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples: Mayo (measuring metabolites by any known process), Alice (intermediated settlement implemented on a generic computer), Benson (BCD-to-binary conversion relevant only to computer). Examiners should ensure claims do more than restate the exception and add the words 'apply it' or merely link to a generic technological environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of breadth versus specificity — claim breadth does not determine eligibility alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring more than mere instructions to apply an exception does not mean a claim must be narrow to be eligible; courts have found both broad claims eligible and narrow claims ineligible depending on whether the claim adds significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: McRO and Thales (broad claims held eligible); Ultramercial and Electric Power Group (narrow claims held ineligible). Focus analysis on whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application or adds significantly more, not solely on claim breadth.
